Every metal on the board ran on Friday morning, and the fastest one ran hardest.

At 5:58am New York, Kitco had gold bid $4,314.50 an ounce, up $75.20 or 1.77%, a fifth consecutive advance. Silver was bid $64.29, up $2.89 or 4.71% — the largest single-session move of the four. Platinum $1,772.00, up 3.14%. Palladium $1,382.00, up 2.14%. Against Thursday's 6:03am mark, gold has added $43.60 an ounce in twenty-four hours and silver $2.62.

Thursday's warning did not hold, and this desk says so. We wrote yesterday that silver turning red beneath a gold high was the clearest internal warning the tape had printed all week, on the reasoning that the high-beta metal leads in both directions. Silver took that back in one session, and the gold to silver ratio tightened to 67.1 from 69.3, more than reversing Thursday's widening. One red session was noise, not a turn. The call is recorded against the print that followed it.

For the bench, fine gold is $138.72 a gram against $137.31 yesterday. Retail quotes are further apart than the spot marks: Khaleej Times had Dubai 24-carat at AED 517.50 a gram this morning, this paper's own metals desk read AED 510.25 the same day, and the overnight desk AED 514.00 on Thursday. A AED 7.25 spread on one session. Both are printed here; neither is picked.

What the trade is pricing is a jobs number. ADP put July private hiring at 44,000 against about 50,000 expected, JOLTS came in softer, claims rose to 199,000, and CME FedWatch has September at 56.9% from 63.4% a week earlier. July non-farm payrolls land at 8:30am, after this edition closed. Quote the timestamp with the price.

The cheapest place a lab-grown diamond now sits is a mall piercing chair.

Claire's is relaunching its in-store piercing experience across the United States and Canada from August 2026, the second revamp of that service in three years. The expanded stud assortment adds lab-grown diamonds and coloured gemstones alongside the existing gold and steel starters. Kits begin at $29.99 with the piercing itself free, and the lab-grown range includes 14-carat white gold studs at 0.10 carats total weight, sold complete with aftercare solution.

The price point is the story rather than the stone. A tenth of a carat of grown material in a gold setting, bundled as a service for a first-time piercing customer, is lab-grown functioning as a finish specification and not as a gemstone purchase. Nobody buying at $29.99 is comparing certificates. They are buying a stud that will not react to a healing lobe, and the material happens to be diamond because grown material has fallen far enough to make that the practical choice at that price.

Which means the competitive damage lands downward, not upward. This is not a natural diamond story. A $29.99 kit competes with cubic zirconia, surgical steel and a twelve-dollar sleeper, and it wins on hypoallergenic setting quality as much as on the stone. The trade should stop reading every new grown price floor as an attack on natural.

The slower effect is the one worth planning for. A generation whose first diamond is a free-with-purchase stud at fourteen arrives at an engagement counter with a different idea of what the word costs. That is a twenty-year problem being created at $29.99 a time, and no amount of certification argument reaches it.

Brilliant Earth sold fewer things for more money, and that was enough to turn the quarter.

Second-quarter revenue rose 6% year on year to $115.1 million on a 2.1% decline in total orders, with average order value up 8% to $2,238. Net income was $0.8 million against a $1.1 million loss in the same quarter last year. Gross margin reached 57.9%, a 360 basis point improvement on the previous quarter. Full-year guidance goes to $459-462 million, with the third quarter guided to roughly flat sales.

The mix is doing the work rather than the traffic. Fine jewellery bookings grew 32% year on year, which is the line that matters most in a business built on bridal, because it is the part of the assortment a customer can buy more than once. An 8% rise in ticket against a 2% fall in orders is a business trading down its unit count deliberately and being paid for it.

A negative order count inside a growing revenue line is worth sitting with. The customer base did not expand. The extra revenue came from existing demand spending more per transaction, which works while the higher-income buyer holds and stops working the moment that cohort trims. The result is concentrated in the top of the company's own customer file — a real strategy, and a narrow one.

For an independent competing against this, the transferable number is the 360 basis point margin recovery. It came from what was sold, not from discounting less, and it is available to any shop willing to edit its case toward pieces that carry a making charge. The figure to watch in the fourth quarter is orders, not revenue: a second consecutive decline with the ticket flat would mean the ticket has finished doing the work.
